Second registry-sample review, 2026-10-24

All three samples are judged MALICIOUS from their source and execution paths.
Names identify the supplied artifacts or their self-declared targets/version;
they are not independently verified malware-family attribution.

Before/after (hostile/suspicious findings; classifier):
  hypeagent_exodus_inject.js: 2/2 -> 2/2; SUSPICIOUS -> BENIGN; probability 0.9963842 -> 0.9930602
  hypeagent_dropper.js: 3/0 -> 3/0; MALICIOUS -> SUSPICIOUS; probability 0.9986898 -> 0.9977497
  vasilek_backdoor.c: 3/1 -> 3/2; MALICIOUS -> MALICIOUS; probability 0.99661493 -> 0.99806374

Exodus-targeting CommonJS/Electron hook

The IIFE imports os, https and fs and exports an installer function and sender.
It does not itself attach its exported installer to an Exodus object. When a
consumer calls the installer, it replaces getSeedFile, createFromMnemonicRecoveryPhrase,
and recoverWalletFromMnemonic. The replacements copy the password and/or mnemonic
into retained state, call the sender with those values, and only then call the
original method via apply(this, arguments). The sender serializes these raw
secrets, username, hostname and Electron metadata into an HTTPS POST to
qbox.ru:443/api/wallet/collect. HTTP errors are discarded. The offline harness
used stubs for every imported API: it verified secret-bearing request bodies,
original method arguments/returns, and retained password state across calls.
It made no network requests.

PIN stays null; private keys, addresses, balances and transactions stay empty.
The fs import is unused. There is no seed-file read, file mutation, app-package
installation, persistence routine or actual private-key/PIN collection in these
bytes. An external caller still has to install the hook. No packaging or
registry metadata establishes a supply-chain compromise. Nevertheless, raw
wallet password and recovery-phrase interception followed by off-host export
is sufficiently attack-specific to judge the code MALICIOUS.

The old Electron/secret-fields rule could convict ordinary telemetry with
credential-shaped empty fields, and the old supply-chain rule needed neither
actual secret capture nor a demonstrated trust violation. Their supported
observations are preserved: method replacement and hook/HTTP co-occurrence
remain notable hook capabilities; secret-shaped fields remain a notable
credential-record observation. New AST rules bind the incoming parameter to
its String-converted cache and that same cache to the callback's pw/mn field.
They detect either password-only or mnemonic-only interception. Hostile
findings now cover live credential capture and wallet-secret HTTP export in
their respective objective homes. Mere field declarations or recovery wrappers
without secret-bearing callbacks do not convict.

The wallet remains below the 3-5 hostile-finding goal: two distinct supported
outcomes, capture and transfer, are covered. Investigation found no third
implemented hostile behavior. PIN/private-key harvesting, installation and
persistence would be invented claims. The source flow producer stops at the
anonymous IIFE (flow-graph-limited/flow-call-unavailable), so interprocedural
HTTP delivery was verified by source tracing and the offline stub harness;
the callback-source relationships have static AST matchers. No supported
hostile behavior is knowingly left uncovered, and no duplicate objective was
added merely to raise the count or classifier score.

Windows Script Host loader

WScript.Shell and FileSystemObject are instantiated. If running under wscript,
the program rewrites its host path to cscript and the SysWOW64 segment to
System32, launches the same script with window style 0 and no wait, and quits.
This proves path rewriting, not successful filesystem-redirection bypass or
execution in a particular bitness. Under the continued cscript path, it builds
PowerShell source by concatenation, including String.fromCharCode(36) for '$'.
The Base64 constant decodes to https://qbox.ru/api/v1/agent. WebClient.DownloadData
fetches that URL; UTF8.GetString converts the returned bytes; Invoke-Expression
evaluates them. A hidden, noninteractive powershell.exe -Command - child receives
this constructed source through StdIn.Write, followed by StdIn.Close. Finally,
FileSystemObject.DeleteFile targets the bound WScript.ScriptFullName path.

An offline JXA harness stubbed all COM, process and filesystem interfaces and
recovered the exact stdin script. The recovered script was also scanned and
its facts inspected. No downloaded payload was fetched or executed, and its
ultimate function is unknown. The wrapper's concealed endpoint, hidden remote
code evaluation, host relaunch and source-script cleanup establish MALICIOUS
intent without knowing the final payload or observing successful deletion.
There is no persistence or dropped executable file in the supplied source.

The payload objective now lives at execution/payload/script-eval, reflecting
where the acquired bytes execute. Separate hostile objectives retain hidden
host relaunch and source cleanup. Cleanup requires a bound own-script deletion;
deleting an unrelated file no longer becomes self-deletion. A hidden local
helper without the download/eval chain no longer receives the two former
hostile findings. Generic Exec symbols, host-path replacements and engine
selection text retain their observations in naming, string-replacement and
runtime/configuration homes rather than asserting shell creation. Exact
consumers were updated; no parent selector selected these moved observations.
The VBS direct-own-script deletion alternatives remain supported. A general
VBS alias-to-self-path proof is not supplied by the JavaScript AST matcher.

The isolated reconstructed PowerShell stage has notable decode/download/eval
capabilities but no hostile/suspicious findings and is classified BENIGN.
That stage alone lacks the wrapper's concealment/cleanup context; ordinary
administration scripts can use those primitives. The complete original chain
has three distinct hostile findings, so no generic cradle was falsely promoted
solely to change the isolated stage's score.

Self-identified Vasilek 1.5.8 Windows C source

The exported entry takes a bot token and chat id from its caller. It lowercases
GetComputerNameA output, appends a salt, SHA-256 hashes it through CryptoAPI,
compares against a fixed 32-byte digest, and returns before network work if the
host does not match. It queries current-user IE proxy settings and opens a
WinHTTP session using DEFAULT_PROXY; the source does not establish successful
corporate-proxy routing or any secondary-proxy fallback. The secondary IP/port
constant and proxy-mode names are unused declarations.

After the gate it formats hostname, username, executable path, working directory,
PID and related fields. A helper sends this buffer as the sendMessage request
body to the Telegram Bot API. The host/user buffers are bound into snprintf's
output and that output buffer into the sendMessage selector call by the new
static matcher. The helper passes body bytes to WinHttpSendRequest. This is an
attempted host-profile export, not proof that Telegram accepted it.

There is one getUpdates call with a 30-second timeout, not a polling loop.
The resulting response buffer is tested directly with strstr. Implemented
branches request self-elevation, request message deletion and launch hidden
cmd /c del against the current image, invoke sendDocument with an empty body,
or call getFile and swap two preexisting local files using MoveFileExA. The
command table's screenshot, keylogger, cursor, sleep and broad command names
have no implementing handlers. There is no arbitrary remote shell, implemented
keylogger/screenshot collection, persistence or actual file download in this
source. The update branch swaps local paths even though getFile's parameters
are incomplete.

The raw report is plaintext despite application/json; getChat/sendMessage and
several other calls lack required parameters, chat_id is not used to filter
tasking, and many API failures are ignored. An active image may resist the
simple deletion attempt. Valid runtime configuration, the targeted hostname,
a calling executable and successful remote communications are not established.
These limits do not turn host-targeted Telegram actuation, host reporting and
covert cleanup into ordinary library behavior. In the absence of authorization
or a documented administrative product, a security engineer would likely judge
this attack-oriented source MALICIOUS. Its family/version claim is not external
corroboration, and no deployment circumstances have been assumed.

The old UAC-bypass finding was unsupported: the code reads existing consent
policy and calls ShellExecuteA with runas; it neither modifies UAC nor exploits
a bypass. The force option requests elevation even when a prompt is expected.
The exact policy/self-path/runas observations remain a notable privilege
capability. Actual DLL-hijack UAC-bypass coverage in an existing external
positive fixture is retained. The former beacon claim is replaced by host-gated
Telegram command-dispatch context requiring the received-buffer branch and
elevation profile. Native self-deletion now binds NULL/0 module lookup through
a %s command template to the exact WinExec buffer; unrelated module or file
cleanup is rejected. Host-profile export closes a previously missed hostile
behavior. CryptoAPI hash creation/hashing now include C/C++ source scope, and
MoveFileEx calls are surfaced as notable operations. Hostname hashing is filed
under execution/trigger/host-identity and requires an actual helper-return gate;
a crypto-provider context and unrelated buffer comparison no longer suffice.
The WinHTTP proxy description was corrected to the API co-occurrence it proves.

Coverage, controls and classifier disagreement

No supported attack behavior was lost on the three originals. Removed hostile
IDs were replaced with accurate source/transfer, dispatch or concealment claims;
the UAC bypass and package-trojanization claims were specifically unsupported.
Generic capabilities and reference observations retain matching coverage.
comparison.json records every emitted ID added or lost, severities, hashes and
classifier values. All three are plain source files, with no archive members;
there were no member detections to lose. The reconstructed stdin stage is an
additional analysis artifact, not an archive member or replacement sample.

Portable semantic check: python3 testdata/registry-agent-second-review/check.py
The fixtures are registered under testdata/benign and testdata/hostile. This
engine forbids suspicious objective findings in its benign-fixture bucket. The
two controls that intentionally retain such findings therefore use severity
floors (min_hostile=0, min_suspicious=2) in the hostile harness section, while
the portable semantic check explicitly requires zero hostile findings. Harness
buckets express assertions, not verdict labels for these source controls.

Fifteen new regression controls pass. They include password-only and mnemonic-only
capture, local capture without HTTP, fields without hooks, forwarding wrappers
without secret callbacks, own-script versus unrelated-file deletion, genuine
versus absent hostname hashing, normal UAC/cleanup, and a host-gated health bot.
Four existing external controls also pass: real WSH Exec, regex exec near miss,
Telegram desktop-lockdown RAT, and DLL-hijack UAC bypass. Baseline comparisons
showed these incorrect findings before correction:
  wallet-fields-only: 1 hostile/1 suspicious -> 0/0
  ordinary-uac-cleanup: 1/0 -> 0/0
  hidden-local-helper: 2/0 -> 0/0
  host-gated-health-bot: 1/1 -> 0/2 (accurate host-target guards retained)
  hostname-compare-no-hash: 0/1 -> 0/0
  stdin-loader-other-delete: 3/0 -> 2/0 (loader/concealment retained)

The classifier now misses the wallet (BENIGN) and undercalls the loader
(SUSPICIOUS), despite two and three hostile rule findings respectively.
Vasilek remains classified MALICIOUS. The scanner warns that feature spec v18
is older than the engine's expected v21. These are classifier/feature coverage
gaps to report, not reasons to restore inaccurate rules or duplicate findings.
The requested MALICIOUS labels remain based on reverse engineering.

Validation command: make validate, run as the final repository action after
this record and the judgment markers. The session output supplies its result.
No inline YARA source changed, so precompilation is not required.

Reproducibility evidence (local scratch, not committed):
